summary:
Busan is a metropolitan city in South Korea and stands under the country's national framework. The source inventory records no Busan-specific ordinance, enforcement pattern or incident series concerning transgender people, so a visitor to the city is assessed against the national picture carried by the South Korea record. Criminalisation, travel-document and marker rules, legal gender recognition and military-service exposure are all national-layer matters.

The one Busan-specific incident in the inventory concerns a public gathering. At Busan's 2018 Pride, some 2,000 police officers were deployed to protect approximately 15,000 attendees from violent anti-gay protesters. The scale of that protective deployment indicates organised, physically threatening opposition to a visible LGBT event in the city. A visitor planning to attend a Pride or a comparable public gathering should expect counter-protest, a heavy police presence and the risk of confrontation around the venue.

Restroom access is not documented as a Busan-specific problem. The litigation source covering police advice to a transitioning person about women's public restrooms records no comparable incident in the city, and no case of a Busan venue barring a transgender person appears in the inventory. Everyday hostility figures available for the country, including harassment and discrimination rates among young people, are national data and are not broken down for Busan.
tangentialFactors:
Restroom litigation in other parts of South Korea sets the comparative baseline. A Korea Times report of 22 July 2024 recorded that an appellate court dismissed the state's appeal and finalised a damages award of 300,000 won on a claim of 3 million won. Police had advised a person transitioning from male to female, who obtained court approval for a family-register gender change in 2020, to avoid women's public restrooms, and the court held that this advice infringed personal rights. The appellate court held that comfortable restroom use is a fundamental and universal human right. No equivalent case has arisen in Busan.

On 8 May 2024 a regional court in Yeongdong approved changing the registered sex from male to female for five transgender applicants who had not had sex-reassignment surgery, holding that it is against the law to determine a gender change by reference to surgery and that court guidelines requiring surgery are now reference rather than criteria. The court stated that every human being has the right to form their character and live a life according to their gender identity. The ruling removed the surgical prerequisite for a registered-sex change and stands as the national framework applied to Busan, although it was handed down by a court in another region.
localsOnly:
A 2021 survey by the National Human Rights Commission of Korea of 591 transgender respondents found that 41% used a restroom of a different gender, 39% avoided food and drink, and 36% went without using a restroom at all. The figures describe a constraint on residents' daily life across the country, including in Busan, rather than any rule set by the city.

Residents hold the same legal position as the plaintiff in the beauty-academy case: in 2021 the Daegu District Court, Pohang branch, awarded 7 million won against an academy that prohibited a transgender student from using its restroom. That precedent binds outside Busan as well, but whether it has been applied to a Busan premises is not documented.

Residents of Busan change their registered sex through the same national court process described in the Yeongdong ruling, and face the same national rules on military service and identity documents as everyone else in the country.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Busan metropolitan ordinance on nondiscrimination, gender identity or restroom access is identified in the inventory, and none is asserted here. Whether the city operates its own human-rights or anti-discrimination instrument is unresolved on the available sources.

The restroom case is described at two court levels. One account reports a first-instance ruling made final on 2 July 2024 with no appeal available, while the Korea Times report of 22 July 2024 describes an appellate court dismissing the state's appeal. Which instance finalised the 300,000 won award is unresolved.

No Busan-specific figures exist in the inventory for violence against transgender people, for police handling of complaints, or for access to transition-related healthcare within the city. The absence of a recorded incident is not evidence that none occurs, and no per-capita or denominator data is supplied for any count cited here.

Whether Busan police have issued restroom, identification or presentation advice comparable to the case documented elsewhere in the country is not sourced.
